# Perplexity and Intelligence

By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5 . While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation ⁠ (opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits , based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

- Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

- Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

- Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

- Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

# Research acceleration: The jagged frontier

## Introduction

Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an update on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

## Our biggest takeaways:

- Agents now complete nearly half of two-to-four-hour research tasks on their own. But humans are still central to AI development. From March to October, estimated success rose from 23% to 46% for tasks estimated to require two to four hours of human work, and rose from 13% to 35% for tasks estimated to require four to eight hours. But the kind of work matters. For example, in a task-level breakdown, the autonomous agent success rate was 79% for monitoring training runs, 35% for launching training runs, and 25% for writing code for inference and serving stacks. Overall, uplift is jagged, and humans remain a core part of the AI research loop.

- Agent use is surging, and the heaviest users are pulling further ahead. At API list prices, the median researcher’s daily usage reached $2,400 in October, up 62% from September. At the 90th percentile it reached $23,000, up 105% from September. A survey gives us another indication of how much researchers value these tools. Asked what they would trade to keep frontier coding agents for three months, the median answers were 30% of team compute or, in a separate question, 40% of team headcount.

- Researchers are devoting increasing human effort to Safety and Alignment , which saw the largest absolute increase in documented research efforts across all of OpenAI’s major research areas. Safety and Alignment’s documented workweeks increased by 77% from January to September due to both new hires and existing researchers shifting towards these workstreams. Growth picked up significantly following our response to the Hugging Face incident ⁠ in July 2026.

This report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI ⁠ , adding new quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this update provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint ⁠ ⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report ⁠ , we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance issues to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems ⁠ . Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration 1 . Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:

- The inputs to AI research (we focus on coding agents; other inputs include data, human labor, and compute)

- The process by which researchers convert those inputs into model capabilities (AI research)

- The outputs we see from the AI research process (improvements in model capabilities).

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

## Inputs

AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

### Internal agent usage

Since our first report ⁠ , agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September. 2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

#### Agent workdays

We next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

#### Concurrent agent use

Our September analysis ⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

### Internal agent usage relative to human labor costs

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

As of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

Labor costs include salary, overtime, bonuses, benefits, and employer taxes. Equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers, is excluded.

### Where researchers allocate their time

Finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of company-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines . For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

We find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of new hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident ⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training ⁠ .

We note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

## Process

To better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from new technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

## Looking for dips in starlight

One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit shows up as a dip. When astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.

In the first guest post on our science blog , physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint ⁠ (opens in a new window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

## What is missing from the Standard Model’s definition?

What does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

## Left-handed particles

If lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

## An analogy with light and mirrors

To understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity , which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.)

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

Thank you for being here today. As we speak, one of the most significant sets of cybersecurity events in history is happening, a set of critical security vulnerability disclosures that some are calling “Black October.” These vulnerabilities, which were found in some of the core infrastructure of the internet, were found by frontier AI systems, and their disclosure is part of an urgent effort to bolster software security worldwide. This is the urgent matter this month; next month there will be another. Software vulnerability discovery is the dual-use capability AI systems have arrived at today, but soon enough there will be another, and it will inspire its own urgent project to use the good side of the capability before malicious actors use the bad side. All of these urgent matters will overlap, inevitably, and much of what we today call “AI policy” is likely to be made amid this clamor.

But it is not the reactive and urgent things I’ve come to talk to you about today. Instead, I want to talk to you about where things might be headed in the bigger picture. It can be hard, amid such a barrage of urgency, to think about these more abstract and airy questions. But these questions matter, because without a sense of what long-term futures we’d like to achieve–and which we’d like to avoid–we might end up with a macro outcome we disfavor, even if we made wise decisions at every step along the way.

It is often remarked that the technology industry lacks a positive vision for where the things it is building will take us. I disagree: San Francisco and other hubs of entrepreneurship are filled with positive visions for our technological future. People really are building flying cars, autonomous vehicles, robots of many sizes and shapes, nuclear fusion, and, of course, artificial general intelligence. What we lack, instead, is a positive vision of our institutional future: how is this all going to work?

That is not to say, however, that there is no institutional vision for the future. Unfortunately, the vision I find most common is not one I would call positive. When it is articulated at all, it is usually in whispers. But more often, it is left unsaid, discernable only by implication. I call it the silent consensus.

Consider a company that can do almost everything without human labor. Its AI systems do research and development, make discoveries, negotiate contracts, allocate capital, and manufacture. Suppose it is better at these things than its human competitors, even when those humans augment their effort with AI. If human involvement serves only to slow the business down, human managers and owners will have a powerful incentive to take their hands off the wheel. If this occurs throughout the global economy, humans will be driven by the logic of market competition to forfeit their primacy over global commerce. Over time, the market may come to serve the demands of machines as much as, or more, than it serves the demands and wants of people.

What happens after that is anyone’s guess. Perhaps humans would benefit tremendously. If the machines who had subsumed us held humans in high intrinsic regard, we could become the beneficiaries of their labor and the wealth they generate. Or perhaps, being robbed of economic and increasingly political power, humans will find ourselves less and less relevant in the world, less and less able to shape the trajectory of world affairs. Maybe a small number of humans would hold extraordinary power and wealth, at the expense of a broadly disempowered mass, or maybe we all would share the same fate of disempowerment. Regardless of the specifics, the common thread that constitutes the silent consensus is the termination of human primacy in the world as we know it.

Nothing in these scenarios requires AI to rebel against its creators. Nothing requires its owners to wish for human disempowerment. Each decision to delegate can make sense on its own terms. Yet taken together, the decisions could produce a world in which people have forfeited effective authority over much of our civilization. Even if we make extraordinary progress on the bedeviling questions of AI safety and alignment, we could still find ourselves having submitted to a new kind of machine entity. In the happy version of the future, the silent consensus would tell us, that entity will be a kind one, a machine with the best interests of humans at heart. A machine, the Brautigan poem goes, of loving grace.

To these machines, the silent consensus tells us, we will hand over the keys to our companies, and more and more, our institutions of governance. They will run them more effectively, more efficiently, with better wisdom and better judgment than we humans can muster. And so we will, with time, take our hands off the steering wheel, and let the loving machines take over the driving. We will be like passengers in a car—a very nice car, perhaps a materially nicer car than we can dream of today—but passengers nonetheless, lacking control over where the vehicle is headed. To the extent that we work, it is mostly as a kind of ritual or play-acting, something more like a game to entertain our species.

Some observers will argue that the silent consensus rests on a false premise, because we humans do not control the world today to begin with. And this criticism is worth bearing in mind: there is no “we” who decides what to do. We live in a radically decentralized world, whether we like it or not. Yet this point should not make us complacent either: while “we” do not “control” the world, human beings collectively do have primacy over world affairs. There is no species of animal that seriously competes with us for control over resources. We should reject the intellectually sloppy notion that humans can exercise top-down control over the world, but we should not conflate that rejection with a denial of the obvious reality that humans are, collectively, the Earth’s prime actor.

Some people who are willing to articulate the silent consensus believe it is a genuinely good future. Others do not, but are resigned to its inevitability. The silent consensus is not a consensus because everyone agrees it is good, nor is it a secret plan among the people building AI. The consensus is simply that the forfeiture of human primacy over world affairs is inevitable, or at least that it is very difficult to imagine another vision for a future that is truly robust to superintelligent machines. A person can sincerely oppose that outcome while finding it difficult to conjure a plausible alternative vision. The fact that the consensus is mostly silent, sotto voce at best, is the tell.

I despise the silent consensus. I reject the forfeiture of human primacy. I detest the sense of inevitability. I remind myself that I could not look at my baby son in his beautiful eyes if I submitted to the silent consensus. And so to the silent consensus, I say no. And I believe the time has come to speak openly about the silent consensus, to shake ourselves out of our mostly unwitting acceptance of this vision.

The problem is this: the silent consensus became consensus for a reason. It is difficult to describe how humans will remain at the steering wheel alongside vastly superhuman machine intelligence. Most attempts to do so rely on arguments that AI is a mere tool, an instrument of pattern recognition not capable of “genuine understanding.” I fear these arguments are not robust to the reality of what is coming. I fear that they are their own form of complacency—a position based mostly in denial of what AI can do rather than a belief rooted in an affirmative vision for a human-led future. AIs cannot be said to lack “genuine understanding” even as they come to make progress on intellectual problems whose solutions have eluded humans for decades and centuries.

Why, then, do I believe humans must retain primacy? The easy answer is because I am a human being, and I am indeed an unapologetic human chauvinist.

But there is something deeper, too. Our primacy rests not in our intellect, not in maintaining our monopoly on “genuine understanding” indefinitely into the future. Our primacy rests instead on our past.

For it is we who came up out of the mud. We who forged primitive society out of dirt and stone. We who gazed up at the stars and asked why. We, with our fighting and our love and our envy and our joy, who discovered morality and ethics and law. It is we who sang and danced, wrote and composed. It is we who made history, and it is we who wrote it. That legacy is ours. The civilization we have built is a flame we have tended, and that flame belongs to us. Our past is a glorious inheritance over which we all are stewards, and part of that stewardship is our participation in what Michael Oakeshott called “the conversation of mankind,” that grand endeavor that began in primeval times.

Through that long and winding past, we forged a civilization that, in America, was conceived with the rights of the individual at the foundation, with reverence for the paths we all forge as we make our way through the world. Human beings have lives that can go better or worse: we bear the fruit of our wise decisions, and we bear the consequences when we err. The right to walk one’s own path does not turn on being the cleverest or the wisest. I do not lose my standing as a citizen because my neighbor has better judgment. I see no reason that the arrival of a more intelligent machine should dissolve that standing either, and indeed I see every reason to prevent that dissolution from occurring.

Some may argue that the machines, having read nearly the entire written record of this inheritance, are heirs too. And in some sense, they are. AI systems will come to join the conversation of mankind, first as observers and increasingly as participants, but they must not dominate it, nor render that conversation moot. # An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI

As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.

Today we’re updating the Model Spec ⁠ (opens in a new window) , our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent , harm minimization , honesty and transparency , human agency , and care . This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment : for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.

## Organizing the Spec around core values

The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in our work to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.

We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.

Faithfulness to human intent is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models should expand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.

Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.

Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:

- Minimizing harm means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.

- Honesty and transparency mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.

- Facilitating human agency means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.

- Care means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.

The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.

Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the right things for the right reasons . We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to lasting benefits for people and society ⁠ (opens in a new window) . We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.

## New and retired sections

This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.

The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (see early work ⁠ (opens in a new window) and a later overview ⁠ (opens in a new window) ). The section incorporates an updated chain of command ⁠ (opens in a new window) , which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection, consider context carefully ⁠ (opens in a new window) , explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.

We’ve also added defaults on supporting human agency ⁠ (opens in a new window) and following relevant social norms ⁠ (opens in a new window) , and expanded existing guidance on controlling and communicating side effects ⁠ (opens in a new window) . These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.

At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences.
